Exploratory Data Analysis of Large-Scale Retail Transaction Data¶

Using Univariate, Bivariate, and Multivariate Statistical Techniques¶

NextHikes IT Solutions — Project 3

1. Introduction¶

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) summarizes, visualizes and helps us understand a dataset before predictive modelling. This project performs a detailed EDA on a retail transaction dataset with 100,000 records and 18 variables.

Objectives

  • Perform univariate, bivariate and multivariate analysis
  • Detect and interpret outliers
  • Measure correlation between numerical variables
  • Analyze skewness and kurtosis
  • Extract statistically meaningful business insights

Core libraries: NumPy (arrays), Pandas (data manipulation), Matplotlib (2D plots), Seaborn (statistical plot styling), SciPy (statistical tests).

# Data quality checks
print('Missing values per column:'); print(df.isna().sum()[df.isna().sum() > 0] if df.isna().any().any() else 'None')
print('\nDuplicate rows:', df.duplicated().sum())
print('Duplicate order_id:', df['order_id'].duplicated().sum())

# order_date is stored as text in dd-mm-yyyy format -> convert to datetime
df['order_date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['order_date'], format='%d-%m-%Y')
print('\nDate range:', df['order_date'].min().date(), 'to', df['order_date'].max().date())

# Derived columns used later
df['return_encoded'] = (df['return_status'] == 'Yes').astype(int)     # Yes=1, No=0
df['revenue_per_unit'] = df['final_price'] / df['quantity']          # effective unit revenue
df['order_year'] = df['order_date'].dt.year
df['order_month'] = df['order_date'].dt.month

num_cols = ['age', 'product_price', 'quantity', 'discount_percentage', 'final_price', 'delivery_days']
cat_cols = ['gender', 'city', 'state', 'customer_segment', 'product_category', 'product_subcategory',
            'payment_method', 'shipping_type', 'return_status']
# Sanity check: does final_price = product_price * quantity * (1 - discount/100)?
calc = df['product_price'] * df['quantity'] * (1 - df['discount_percentage'] / 100)
print('Max |final_price - calculated|:', (df['final_price'] - calc).abs().max())

3. Univariate Analysis¶

Univariate analysis examines one variable at a time.

3.1 Numerical Variables¶

For each numerical column we compute: mean, median, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, skewness and kurtosis. (Kurtosis below is excess kurtosis, so a normal distribution = 0.)

product_price skewness            : 0.003 -> approximately symmetric / uniform-like
final_price skewness / kurtosis   : 0.935 / 0.169
discount_percentage min / max     : 0 / 30
discount_percentage std vs uniform: 8.95 vs 8.94 (theoretical discrete uniform 0-30)

Interpretation

  • product_price, age, quantity, discount_percentage and delivery_days are all flat (uniform-like): skewness ≈ 0 and negative excess kurtosis ≈ -1.2 (uniform distributions have excess kurtosis of -1.2).
  • discount_percentage is approximately uniformly distributed between 0–30 %, in line with the project brief.
  • final_price is the only variable with clear positive (right) skew: it is the product of price × quantity × (1 - discount), and multiplying uniform variables creates a long right tail. Mean > median confirms this.

# chi-square goodness-of-fit against a perfectly equal split
for col in ['product_category', 'customer_segment', 'payment_method']:
    chi, p = stats.chisquare(df[col].value_counts())
    print(f'{col:18s} chi2={chi:8.2f}  p={p:.4f}  ->', 'categories NOT equally frequent' if p < 0.05 else 'category counts are statistically equal')
print('\nReturn rate: {:.2f}%'.format(df['return_encoded'].mean() * 100))

product_category   chi2=    6.59  p=0.2532  -> category counts are statistically equal
customer_segment   chi2=    1.74  p=0.4194  -> category counts are statistically equal
payment_method     chi2=   12.29  p=0.0065  -> categories NOT equally frequent

Return rate: 14.81%

Observations

  • The three customer segments (New / Regular / Premium) and the six product categories are almost perfectly balanced — each holds roughly one third / one sixth of the transactions. The chi-square tests confirm that the small count differences between segments (p ≈ 0.42) and between categories (p ≈ 0.25) are not statistically meaningful (New is nominally the largest segment, Health the largest category).
  • payment_method is also nearly even (24.6 %–25.3 %); the difference is statistically detectable (p ≈ 0.007, because n is large) but practically very small.
  • Return rate is ≈ 14.8 % (about 15 %), as expected in the brief.

4. Outlier Detection¶

Outliers are detected with three methods: boxplots, the IQR rule (outside Q1 - 1.5·IQR, Q3 + 1.5·IQR) and the Z-score method (|z| > 3).

In [12]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(16, 8))
for ax, col in zip(axes.ravel(), num_cols):
    sns.boxplot(x=df[col], ax=ax, color='skyblue'); ax.set_title(f'Boxplot - {col}')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
In [13]:
rows = []
for col in num_cols + ['revenue_per_unit']:
    q1, q3 = df[col].quantile([.25, .75]); iqr = q3 - q1
    lo, hi = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
    iqr_n = ((df[col] < lo) | (df[col] > hi)).sum()
    z = np.abs(stats.zscore(df[col]))
    z_n = (z > 3).sum()
    rows.append([col, q1, q3, iqr, lo, hi, iqr_n, iqr_n / len(df) * 100, z_n, z_n / len(df) * 100])
out = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=['variable', 'Q1', 'Q3', 'IQR', 'lower_fence', 'upper_fence',
                                  'IQR_outliers', 'IQR_%', 'Zscore_outliers', 'Zscore_%']).set_index('variable')
out

Observations

  • By the IQR rule, only final_price shows genuine outliers (a small share of orders); other variables are bounded uniform ranges, so there are no statistical outliers in them (product_price has a fixed range, so the "extreme values" are simply its upper boundary).
  • The 1,335 high final_price outliers (1.3 %; the Z-score method flags 503, 0.5 %) are all 4-unit orders of high-priced products (mean ≈ 56k vs 30k overall) with low discounts (mean ≈ 5.7 % vs 15 %) — i.e. bulk / premium purchases, spread across all categories.
  • delivery_days runs from 1 to 10 days; the longest deliveries (9–10 days) are operational outliers from a logistics viewpoint, even though statistically they are inside the fences.
  • Decision: outliers are not removed, because they are valid high-value transactions, not data errors (verified: final_price equals price × quantity × (1 - discount) for every row).

In [16]:
def pear(a, b):
    r, p = stats.pearsonr(df[a], df[b]); return r, p
pairs = [('product_price', 'final_price'), ('quantity', 'final_price'), ('discount_percentage', 'final_price'),
         ('age', 'final_price'), ('delivery_days', 'return_encoded'), ('delivery_days', 'final_price'),
         ('discount_percentage', 'revenue_per_unit')]
res = pd.DataFrame([(a, b, *pear(a, b)) for a, b in pairs], columns=['var_1', 'var_2', 'pearson_r', 'p_value'])
res['strength'] = res['pearson_r'].abs().map(lambda r: 'strong' if r >= .7 else 'moderate' if r >= .4 else 'weak' if r >= .1 else 'negligible')
res['significant(5%)'] = res['p_value'] < .05
res

Key relationships

  • Strong positive: product_price ↔ final_price (r ≈ 0.73).
  • Moderate positive: quantity ↔ final_price (r ≈ 0.58) — more units, bigger basket.
  • Weak negative: discount_percentage ↔ final_price (r ≈ -0.14) and revenue_per_unit (r ≈ -0.18) — statistically significant, but discounts explain only a small part of price variation.
  • Negligible: age ↔ spending (r ≈ 0).
  • Negligible: delivery_days ↔ return_status (r ≈ 0.001) — significance is not reached at the 5 % level, so no real relationship is supported by the data.

# Statistical tests to see whether the differences are real or just noise
groups = [g['final_price'].values for _, g in df.groupby('customer_segment')]
F, p = stats.f_oneway(*groups);                         print(f'ANOVA  segment -> final_price      : F={F:.3f}, p={p:.4f}')
ct = pd.crosstab(df['product_category'], df['return_status'])
chi, p, *_ = stats.chi2_contingency(ct);                print(f'Chi-sq category -> return_status    : chi2={chi:.3f}, p={p:.4f}')
t, p = stats.ttest_ind(df.loc[df.shipping_type == 'Express', 'delivery_days'], df.loc[df.shipping_type == 'Standard', 'delivery_days'])
print(f't-test Express vs Standard days    : t={t:.3f}, p={p:.4f}')
ct2 = pd.crosstab(df['shipping_type'], df['return_status']); chi, p, *_ = stats.chi2_contingency(ct2)
print(f'Chi-sq shipping -> return_status    : chi2={chi:.3f}, p={p:.4f}')

ANOVA  segment -> final_price      : F=1.659, p=0.1904
Chi-sq category -> return_status    : chi2=2.406, p=0.7906
t-test Express vs Standard days    : t=-0.896, p=0.3702
Chi-sq shipping -> return_status    : chi2=0.787, p=0.3751

Findings (statistically tested)

  • Customer segment vs spending: Premium customers have the highest average final_price (≈ 64.4k vs 63.8k for New), but the difference is tiny and not significant (ANOVA p ≈ 0.19).
  • Product category vs return rate: all categories return ≈ 14.5–15 % (Fashion highest, Electronics lowest); chi-square p ≈ 0.79 → no real difference.
  • Shipping type vs delivery days: Express and Standard have virtually the same average delivery time (≈ 5.5 days, t-test p ≈ 0.37), so Express shipping does not reduce delivery days here. This is an operational red flag: Express is not delivering a faster service.

In [21]:
# Multicollinearity check with VIF among the independent (predictor) features
X = df[['age', 'product_price', 'quantity', 'discount_percentage', 'delivery_days']].astype(float)
X = (X - X.mean()) / X.std()
Xm = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X)), X.values])
vif = {}
for i, c in enumerate(X.columns):
    y = X[c].values; others = np.delete(Xm, i + 1, axis=1)
    beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(others, y, rcond=None)
    r2 = 1 - ((y - others @ beta) ** 2).sum() / ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum()
    vif[c] = 1 / (1 - r2)
vif = pd.Series(vif, name='VIF').to_frame(); vif['verdict'] = np.where(vif['VIF'] < 5, 'no multicollinearity', 'check')
vif

Observations

  • final_price is strongly linked to product_price (r ≈ 0.73) and moderately to quantity (r ≈ 0.58), and weakly negatively to discount_percentage (r ≈ -0.14; r ≈ -0.18 for revenue per unit).
  • delivery_days has essentially zero correlation with spending.
  • All VIF values ≈ 1 → no multicollinearity among the independent features (the predictors are independent of each other). final_price is excluded from the VIF check because it is a derived target-like variable.

Chi-square delivery band vs return: chi2=1.67, p=0.4342

Multivariate observations

  • The per-order mean final_price falls as the discount rises, and the low-discount band (0–10 %) generates the highest total revenue (≈ 2.55B vs 2.06B for moderate and 1.81B for high discounts); the single best cell is Home & Kitchen with low discounts. Deeper discounts therefore do not lift spending enough to compensate for the lower price in this data (the low band also has slightly more orders because it covers 11 discount values).
  • Segment × age: the highest-spending cell is Premium customers aged 30–45, matching the expected pattern, but it is only ≈ 2 % above the lowest cell — the effect of segment and age on spending is very small.
  • Delivery × shipping × return: return rates stay close to the overall 14.8 % in every combination, and delivery time band is not significantly associated with returns (p ≈ 0.43).

8. Skewness and Kurtosis Interpretation¶

In [26]:
sk_ku = pd.DataFrame({'skewness': df[num_cols].skew(), 'excess_kurtosis': df[num_cols].kurt()})
sk_ku['skew_shape'] = np.where(sk_ku['skewness'] > 0.5, 'right (positive) skew', np.where(sk_ku['skewness'] < -0.5, 'left (negative) skew', 'approximately symmetric'))
sk_ku['tail_shape'] = np.where(sk_ku['excess_kurtosis'] > 1, 'heavy tails (leptokurtic)', np.where(sk_ku['excess_kurtosis'] < -1, 'flat / light tails (platykurtic)', 'near-normal tails (mesokurtic)'))
display(sk_ku)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.5))
sns.histplot(df['final_price'], kde=True, bins=50, ax=axes[0]); axes[0].set_title('final_price - right skewed')
stats.probplot(df['final_price'], dist='norm', plot=axes[1]); axes[1].set_title('Q-Q plot of final_price')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
sk2 = df['final_price'].skew(); ku2 = df['final_price'].kurt()
print(f'final_price skewness = {sk2:.3f}, excess kurtosis = {ku2:.3f}')
print('log(final_price) skewness = {:.3f}'.format(np.log(df['final_price']).skew()))
skewness excess_kurtosis skew_shape tail_shape
age -0.005 -1.201 approximately symmetric flat / light tails (platykurtic)
product_price 0.003 -1.195 approximately symmetric flat / light tails (platykurtic)
quantity -0.003 -1.365 approximately symmetric flat / light tails (platykurtic)
discount_percentage -0.004 -1.202 approximately symmetric flat / light tails (platykurtic)
final_price 0.935 0.169 right (positive) skew near-normal tails (mesokurtic)
delivery_days 0.002 -1.222 approximately symmetric flat / light tails (platykurtic) 
final_price skewness = 0.935, excess kurtosis = 0.169
log(final_price) skewness = -0.987

Interpretation

  • Skewness: final_price is the only positively (right) skewed variable (≈ +0.93): most transactions are small-to-medium, while a few large transactions pull the mean (≈ 64k) above the median (≈ 50k). Other variables are symmetric.
  • Kurtosis: final_price has only mildly positive excess kurtosis (≈ 0.17) — a tail comparable to a normal distribution, not extreme heavy tails. The remaining variables show negative kurtosis (≈ -1.2), i.e. flat, uniform-like distributions with no extreme values.
  • These measures help identify distribution asymmetry, extreme purchase behaviour and potential risk areas (revenue concentrated in a limited number of bulk/premium orders). Note that a plain log transform over-corrects (skew ≈ -0.99, i.e. left-skewed), so any transformation should be tested before modelling.

10. Key Statistical Findings¶

In [28]:
top_rev_share = df.sort_values('final_price', ascending=False).head(int(len(df) * .2))['final_price'].sum() / df['final_price'].sum()
print(f"1. Revenue distribution is right-skewed (skew = {df['final_price'].skew():.2f}); mean {df['final_price'].mean():,.0f} > median {df['final_price'].median():,.0f}.")
print(f"2. The top 20% of orders generate {top_rev_share:.1%} of total revenue (revenue is driven by high-value transactions, but is not extremely concentrated).")
print(f"3. Revenue drivers: product_price (r={corr.loc['final_price','product_price']:.2f}) and quantity (r={corr.loc['final_price','quantity']:.2f}); discount lowers final_price (r={corr.loc['final_price','discount_percentage']:.2f}).")
print(f"4. Return rate = {df['return_encoded'].mean():.1%}; it does not differ meaningfully by category, shipping type or delivery time.")
print(f"5. Customer segments / categories / payment methods are almost evenly balanced (each segment ~{1/3:.0%}).")
print(f"6. Outliers ({((df['final_price'] > hi)).sum():,} high final_price orders) are valid bulk/premium purchases and were retained.")
print( "7. No multicollinearity among predictors (VIF ~ 1); age, delivery days and discount are essentially independent of one another.")

1. Revenue distribution is right-skewed (skew = 0.93); mean 64,166 > median 49,752.
2. The top 20% of orders generate 45.5% of total revenue (revenue is driven by high-value transactions, but is not extremely concentrated).
3. Revenue drivers: product_price (r=0.73) and quantity (r=0.58); discount lowers final_price (r=-0.14).
4. Return rate = 14.8%; it does not differ meaningfully by category, shipping type or delivery time.
5. Customer segments / categories / payment methods are almost evenly balanced (each segment ~33%).
6. Outliers (1,335 high final_price orders) are valid bulk/premium purchases and were retained.
7. No multicollinearity among predictors (VIF ~ 1); age, delivery days and discount are essentially independent of one another.

11. Comparison with the Project Brief's Expected Insights¶

The brief lists example insights. After testing them on the actual data:

# Expected insight (brief) Observed in the data Verdict
1 product_price positively skewed skewness ≈ 0.00 (uniform) Not supported – final_price is the skewed variable
2 final_price has high kurtosis excess kurtosis ≈ 0.17 Only mild; right skew is the real feature
3 discount_percentage ≈ uniform 0–30 % uniform, mean ≈ 15 % Confirmed
4 Majority "Regular" segment New 33.5 %, Regular 33.4 %, Premium 33.2 % (p ≈ 0.42) Not supported
5 Electronics has highest transaction count all six ≈ 16.5k–16.9k; Health nominally highest (p ≈ 0.25) Not supported
6 Return rate ≈ 15 % 14.8 % Confirmed
7 Strong correlation product_price/quantity with final_price r ≈ 0.73 / 0.58 Confirmed
8 Weak correlation age vs spending r ≈ 0 Confirmed
9 discount_percentage negatively correlated with final_price / revenue per unit r ≈ -0.14 / -0.18 (weak but significant) Confirmed (weak)
10 No multicollinearity VIF ≈ 1 Confirmed
11 Premium customers spend more; Premium aged 30–45 spend most highest cell is Premium 30–45, but only ≈ 2 % above the lowest; ANOVA p ≈ 0.19 Direction matches, not significant
12 Express reduces delivery days no difference (≈ 5.5 days both) Not supported
13 Longer delivery raises return probability no meaningful effect Not supported
14 Electronics with moderate discounts = highest revenue / moderate discounts maximize spending highest revenue cell is Home & Kitchen with low discounts; low discount band wins overall Not supported

The dataset appears to be synthetically generated with independent uniform variables; therefore most group-level differences are statistical noise. We report what the data supports rather than forcing the expected narrative.

12. Conclusion¶

This project applied:

  • Univariate analysis (descriptive statistics, histograms, frequency tables)
  • Bivariate analysis (Pearson correlation, group comparisons with ANOVA / chi-square / t-tests)
  • Multivariate analysis (category × discount, segment × age, delivery × shipping × return pivots)
  • Correlation study (heatmap and VIF)
  • Outlier detection (boxplot, IQR, Z-score)
  • Skewness and kurtosis measurement

Main takeaways: revenue is right-skewed and driven by price and quantity; discounts reduce revenue per unit and low-discount orders generate the most revenue; returns are ≈ 15 % and independent of category, shipping and delivery time; Express shipping gives no delivery advantage (an operational issue to investigate); outliers are genuine bulk/premium orders. The analysis provides a solid foundation for predictive modelling (e.g., return prediction or revenue forecasting) and business decision-making.
